days.guide: The child writes a one-page informative profile: introduction, what the person did, the risks and results, and a conclusion, with in-text citations and a works-cited list. Before moving on, ask: "What is an upstander?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is an upstander?
questions.a: Someone who acts to help others facing injustice.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test on drama terms, the play and the nonfiction texts. Afterward the child corrects misses using the play text.

questions.q: Define foil.
questions.a: A character who contrasts with another to highlight traits.

weeks.assessment_key: Research profile rubric (4 levels): accurate facts from 3 cited sources about one upstander — e.g., Miep Gies helped hide the Franks and saved Anne's diary; Irena Sendler smuggled about 2,500 Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto; Chiune Sugihara, Japanese diplomat in Lithuania, issued transit visas in 1940 that saved thousands; organized, in own words, with MLA citations. Unit 6 test: drama terms (stage direction, dramatic irony, foil, epilogue), play events, Wiesel's claim.

weeks.prep: Print Ovid's 'Pyramus and Thisbe' (Metamorphoses Book IV, Project Gutenberg translation).
misconceptions: Thinking Shakespeare invented the star-crossed lovers pattern. It goes back to ancient myth.
Confusing archetype with stereotype. An archetype is a recurring pattern across literature.

days.guide: Read the myth aloud together. The child lists the 8 key events in order.

questions.q: Give the 8 key events.
questions.a: Neighbors Pyramus and Thisbe fall in love in Babylon; their parents forbid it; they whisper through a crack in the wall; they plan to meet at Ninus's tomb under a white mulberry tree; Thisbe arrives first and flees a lioness, dropping her veil; the lioness bloodies the veil; Pyramus finds it, thinks she's dead and kills himself with his sword; Thisbe returns, finds him and kills herself — the berries turn dark red forever.

days.guide: Define archetype as a pattern that recurs across many stories and cultures. The child lists the star-crossed lovers, forbidden love and tragic misunderstanding patterns in Ovid and names another story that uses each.

questions.q: Name the archetypal patterns.
questions.a: Star-crossed lovers, forbidden love, tragic misunderstanding.

days.guide: Tell the short myths of Narcissus, Echo and Tantalus. The child defines narcissism, echo and tantalize, explains each word's origin, and writes one original sentence for each.

questions.q: What does 'tantalize' mean and where does it come from?
questions.a: To tease with something out of reach; from Tantalus.

days.guide: Summarize Romeo and Juliet briefly if the child doesn't know it. The child makes a three-column chart (Ovid / Romeo and Juliet / a modern story or film) for obstacle, secret meeting, misunderstanding and ending.

questions.q: What does Romeo and Juliet share with Ovid?
questions.a: Feuding/forbidding families, secret love, a misunderstanding about death, double suicide.

days.guide: Give the myth-vocabulary quiz (key). Have the child correct misses by writing the myth behind each word.

questions.q: What is a metamorphosis in the myth?
questions.a: The mulberries change from white to dark red.

weeks.assessment_key: Myth vocabulary quiz: narcissism (excessive self-love; from Narcissus, who fell in love with his reflection); echo (from the nymph Echo who could only repeat others' words); tantalize (from Tantalus, punished with food and water always just out of reach); metamorphosis (transformation); archetype; allusion. 1 point each plus a sentence using each correctly.

weeks.prep: Use the free Folger Shakespeare edition of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' (folger.edu) and a Folger video on the Globe Theatre. Read Acts 1–2 yourself; a plot summary (Folger synopsis) helps.
misconceptions: Thinking 'wherefore' or 'thou' make the language impossible. Paraphrase line by line with Folger's notes.
Losing track of the lovers. Keep a character map with arrows for who loves whom and update it after each potion.

days.guide: Watch the Globe video, then read Act 1, Scene 1; child paraphrases Egeus's complaint and Hermia's choice. Finish by asking: "What is Hermia's choice?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is Hermia's choice?
questions.a: Marry Demetrius as her father demands, be put to death, or become a nun — 'to abjure forever the society of men.'

questions.q: What does 'The course of true love never did run smooth' mean?
questions.a: True love always faces obstacles — said by Lysander.

days.guide: Read Act 1, Scene 2 aloud with funny voices for the mechanicals. The child lists each mechanical's assigned role and what Bottom's eagerness shows about him.

questions.q: Which roles are assigned?
questions.a: Bottom: Pyramus; Flute: Thisbe; Snug: the Lion; Starveling: Thisbe's mother; Snout: Pyramus's father; Quince: Thisbe's father.

questions.q: What does Bottom's eagerness reveal?
questions.a: He's overconfident and comic — he wants to play every part, including Thisbe and the Lion.

days.guide: Read Act 2 (summarize long fairy speeches if needed). The child draws a love map with arrows before and after Puck's mistake.

questions.q: Who loves whom after Puck's mistake?
questions.a: Before: Lysander and Demetrius both love Hermia; Hermia loves Lysander; Helena loves Demetrius. After Puck anoints Lysander: Lysander loves Helena, Demetrius still loves Hermia, Hermia loves Lysander, Helena loves Demetrius — no one's love is returned.

days.guide: Clap da-DUM five times while reading 'The course of true love never did run smooth.' The child marks stresses in 4 lines and explains 5 puns or ironic lines in plain English. To check, ask: "What is iambic pentameter?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What is iambic pentameter?
questions.a: Ten syllables per line in five da-DUM beats.

days.guide: Give the Acts 1–2 quiz, then the 10-line paraphrase task. Check that the paraphrase keeps every idea.

questions.q: Who is Puck?
questions.a: Robin Goodfellow, Oberon's mischievous servant.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz Acts 1–2: 1) Egeus wants Hermia to marry Demetrius; Athenian law says she must obey, die, or become a nun. 2) Hermia loves Lysander; they plan to flee through the woods. 3) Helena loves Demetrius and tells him of the plan. 4) The mechanicals: Bottom = Pyramus, Flute = Thisbe, Snug = Lion. 5) Oberon and Titania quarrel over a changeling boy. 6) Puck puts the potion on Lysander by mistake; he wakes loving Helena. Paraphrase task: score for accuracy of meaning (2), modern English (1), no omitted ideas (1).

weeks.prep: Read Acts 3–4 (Folger). Prepare a three-column chart: Athenian court / lovers / mechanicals & fairies.
misconceptions: Thinking the comedy is random. The confusion follows from specific mistakes (Puck's potion) and is resolved by Oberon.
Confusing subplot with main plot.

days.guide: Read Act 3, Scene 1 aloud; let the child read Bottom. Ask what the audience knows that Bottom does not and why that makes the scene funny.

questions.q: Why is the scene funny?
questions.a: Bottom has an ass's head but doesn't know it, while the queen of fairies adores him — dramatic irony.

questions.q: What wise line does Bottom say?
questions.a: 'Reason and love keep little company together nowadays.'

days.guide: Read Act 3, Scene 2, tracking how Puck's mistake and Oberon's fix make both men love Helena. Act out the Hermia–Helena insult exchange with exaggerated expression.

questions.q: Why does Helena think everyone mocks her?
questions.a: Now both men claim to love her, which she thinks is a cruel joke.

questions.q: Give an insult.
questions.a: Helena calls Hermia 'puppet'; Hermia calls her a 'painted maypole.'

days.guide: Read Act 4. The child explains step by step how Oberon restores order and paraphrases Bottom's speech about his 'most rare vision.'

questions.q: How does order return?
questions.a: Titania gives up the boy, Oberon frees her, Puck removes Bottom's head, Demetrius stays in love with Helena, and Theseus overrules Egeus.

days.guide: The child completes the three-column chart showing each plotline's conflict, where it crosses the others in the woods, and how it resolves. Finish by asking: "Where do the plots cross?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Where do the plots cross?
questions.a: In the woods.

days.guide: Give the Acts 3–4 quiz with a short response explaining one example of dramatic irony. Before moving on, ask: "What is Bottom's vision?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is Bottom's vision?
questions.a: He thinks he had a strange dream.

weeks.assessment_key: Plot structure chart: each column shows the conflict (Theseus's wedding & Egeus's demand; the four lovers' tangle; Oberon–Titania quarrel & mechanicals' play), how they cross in the woods, and the resolution (Oberon frees Titania, lovers paired correctly, Theseus overrules Egeus, triple wedding, mechanicals' play chosen). Quiz: Puck gives Bottom an ass's head; Titania loves Bottom; Oberon anoints Demetrius, who loves Helena; Hermia and Helena quarrel; Puck fixes Lysander; Bottom's 'most rare vision.' Short response: dramatic irony — we know Bottom has an ass's head while he doesn't.

weeks.prep: Read Act 5 and reread Ovid's 'Pyramus and Thisbe.' Gather simple props (a lantern for Moonshine, a sign for Wall, a toy sword).
misconceptions: Thinking parody means mockery of the original story's value. Shakespeare parodies bad acting and over-the-top tragedy while honoring the source.
Listing differences without explaining effects. Always add 'which makes the audience...'

days.guide: Read Act 5's 'Pyramus and Thisbe' aloud with Ovid's version beside it. The child lists ways it parodies Ovid's tragic tone (Wall, Moonshine, the Lion, Pyramus's overlong death).

questions.q: How do the Wall and Moonshine parody Ovid?
questions.a: Actors literally play the wall (Snout holding up fingers for the chink) and moonlight (Starveling with a lantern, thorn bush and dog), turning tragic setting into silliness.

days.guide: The child charts what Shakespeare keeps from Ovid and what he changes, adding the effect of each change on the audience. To check, ask: "What is kept from Ovid?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What is kept from Ovid?
questions.a: The wall, the meeting at Ninus's tomb, the lion, the bloody mantle, the double suicide.

days.guide: Model a thesis about transformation. The child drafts a 4-paragraph essay with quotations from both texts.

questions.q: What does 'rendered new' mean?
questions.a: Turning old material into a new form with new purpose.

days.guide: The child rehearses Bottom as Pyramus or Puck's epilogue with simple props, then performs for family with clear diction and gestures. Before moving on, ask: "Puck's epilogue begins?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Puck's epilogue begins?
questions.a: 'If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended.'

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test on myth and Shakespeare and collect the revised essay. Check understanding with: "Define play within a play." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Define play within a play.
questions.a: A performance staged inside a play.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison essay rubric (4 levels): thesis on how Shakespeare transforms Ovid's tragedy into comedy; evidence from both texts (e.g., Ovid's crack in the wall vs Snout playing Wall and holding up his fingers as the 'chink'; Ovid's terrifying lioness vs Snug reassuring the ladies he's just a joiner; Pyramus's death 'Now die, die, die, die, die'); commentary; conventions. Performance rubric: memorized or fluent, clear diction, gestures, props. Unit 7 test: myth terms, play events, iambic pentameter, dramatic irony, parody.

weeks.prep: Library card for online databases; Purdue OWL; research notebook. Suggest topics: printing press, vaccines, transcontinental railroad.
misconceptions: Choosing too broad a topic. Narrow to a question that can be answered in 4–6 pages.
Trusting the first search result. Evaluate every source.

days.guide: Brainstorm 8–10 innovations together and talk through which interest the child most. The child picks one and lists what he or she already knows and wonders.

questions.q: What makes a good research topic?
questions.a: Interesting, narrow enough, with available sources.

days.guide: Model narrowing a broad topic to a question. The child writes a focused research question and 5 sub-questions; give feedback on scope.

questions.q: Narrow 'vaccines.'
questions.a: 'How did Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine lead to smallpox eradication?'

days.guide: Show the library's databases (e.g., Gale, Britannica School) and search operators (quotation marks, site:, minus sign). The child finds 6 possible sources and logs them.

questions.q: What does putting quotation marks around words in a search do?
questions.a: Searches for that exact phrase.

questions.q: What does site:.gov do?
questions.a: Limits results to government websites.

days.guide: Model the CRAAP test on one source. The child scores each source and keeps the 4 most credible, noting why.

questions.q: What does CRAAP stand for?
questions.a: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

days.guide: The child submits a one-page proposal: question, sub-questions, 4 sources and a working MLA bibliography. To check, ask: "Primary vs secondary source?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Primary vs secondary source?
questions.a: Primary is firsthand from the time; secondary analyzes it later.

weeks.assessment_key: Research proposal rubric: focused question; 5 sub-questions; 4 credible sources (mix of primary and secondary) with CRAAP notes; working bibliography in MLA (1 point per element). Example question: 'How did the printing press change the spread of ideas in 16th-century Europe?'

weeks.prep: Note cards (or a digital notes document), the child's 4 sources, Purdue OWL MLA guide (owl.purdue.edu). Pick 5 short passages from the child's sources for paraphrase practice.
misconceptions: Thinking paraphrases and summaries don't need citations. Any borrowed idea or fact that isn't common knowledge must be cited.
Patchwriting — swapping a few synonyms while keeping the original sentence structure. That is still plagiarism.

days.guide: Model one note card: heading (sub-question), fact in own words or quoted, source code and page. Child takes notes from at least two sources, organized by sub-question.

questions.q: What must every note include?
questions.a: The source and page (or paragraph/URL) so it can be cited later.

days.guide: Model the 'read, cover, write, check' paraphrase method. Child paraphrases 5 passages and compares each to the original for borrowed phrases.

questions.q: Original: 'Gutenberg's press could print thousands of pages a day.' Give an acceptable paraphrase.
questions.a: Example: 'With Gutenberg's invention, printers could produce pages by the thousands every day' — plus a citation.

days.guide: Teach signal phrases ('According to ...,' 'Historian X argues ...') and ellipses for omissions. Child integrates 5 quotations.

questions.q: Fix this dropped quotation: 'The printing press mattered. "It spread ideas quickly."'
questions.a: 'According to historian Elizabeth Eisenstein, the press "spread ideas quickly" (45).' — introduce with a signal phrase and cite. [example]

days.guide: Using Purdue OWL, child formats 4 works-cited entries and checks each against the model. To check, ask: "Give the MLA pattern for a book." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Give the MLA pattern for a book.
questions.a: Last, First. Title in Italics. Publisher, Year.

days.guide: Collect notes and works cited; give the short plagiarism quiz (key). Finish by asking: "Is it plagiarism to reuse your own old essay without permission?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Is it plagiarism to reuse your own old essay without permission?
questions.a: Yes, in most classes — 'self-plagiarism' — unless the teacher allows it.

weeks.assessment_key: Notes: every card has a sub-question heading, one fact or idea, source and page (1 point per 5 complete cards). Works cited (MLA 9): alphabetical by author's last name, hanging indent, double-spaced, each entry with author, title, container, publisher/date, URL or pages as available. Plagiarism quiz answers: 1) Must you cite a paraphrase? Yes. 2) Must you cite 'George Washington was the first U.S. president'? No — common knowledge. 3) Is changing a few words of a sentence acceptable without quotation marks? No — patchwriting. 4) Where does an in-text citation go? At the end of the sentence, before the period: (Smith 42).

weeks.prep: Notes, an outline template, a word processor. Plan four writing sessions; the paper is 4–6 pages.
misconceptions: Writing one paragraph per source ('Source 1 says...'). Synthesis organizes paragraphs by idea and combines several sources in each.
Informal style (contractions, 'you,' slang). Use formal, third-person academic voice.

days.guide: Child builds an outline: thesis, 3–4 sections, each with notes from at least two sources. Check that every section supports the thesis.

questions.q: Turn the question 'How did the printing press change Europe?' into a thesis.
questions.a: Example: 'The printing press transformed Europe by spreading literacy, fueling the Reformation, and accelerating scientific exchange.'

days.guide: Child drafts the introduction and first two sections with in-text citations; remind them to keep moving and fix later. Check understanding with: "Where does an MLA in-text citation go?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where does an MLA in-text citation go?
questions.a: At the end of the sentence before the period, e.g., (Eisenstein 45).

days.guide: Child drafts the remaining sections and the conclusion. To check, ask: "What should a research conclusion do?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What should a research conclusion do?
questions.a: Restate the thesis in new words, pull the main points together and explain why the topic matters today.

days.guide: Revise together for synthesis, formal style and precise vocabulary: highlight each source in a different color to see whether paragraphs combine sources. Finish by asking: "Give a formal replacement for 'a lot of people thought.'" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Give a formal replacement for 'a lot of people thought.'
questions.a: 'Many contemporaries believed...'

days.guide: Child edits punctuation and citation format, formats the works-cited page, and publishes the final paper. Before moving on, ask: "Does the works-cited page count toward the 4–6 pages?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Does the works-cited page count toward the 4–6 pages?
questions.a: Usually not — it's a separate final page.

weeks.assessment_key: Research paper rubric (4 levels per trait): Thesis (clear, answers the research question); Organization (logical sections, topic sentences, transitions); Evidence & synthesis (multiple sources per section, quotations and paraphrases integrated); Citation (every borrowed idea cited; in-text citations match the works cited); Style (formal, precise vocabulary); Conventions; Length 4–6 pages.

weeks.prep: Slide software (Google Slides, PowerPoint or Keynote), image sources with licenses (e.g., Wikimedia Commons, Library of Congress), a timer and a phone to record rehearsal. Invite an audience for Thursday.
misconceptions: Putting paragraphs on slides and reading them. Slides should show images, a chart or key words; the speaker explains.
Using any image from a search without credit. Credit the creator and source on the slide or a credits slide.

days.guide: Child plans a 5-minute talk: hook, thesis, 3 key points with one piece of evidence each, conclusion. Check understanding with: "About how many words fit in a 5-minute talk?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: About how many words fit in a 5-minute talk?
questions.a: Roughly 600–700 words at a natural speaking pace.

days.guide: Child builds slides with images, one chart or timeline and minimal text, crediting each image. To check, ask: "A good guideline for text per slide?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A good guideline for text per slide?
questions.a: A title plus a few key words — about 6 words per line and no more than 3–4 lines.

days.guide: Rehearse with a timer and record. Watch together and note one strength and one fix for eye contact, volume and pacing.

questions.q: What are filler words and how do you reduce them?
questions.a: 'Um,' 'like,' 'so' — pause silently instead and practice transitions.

days.guide: Child presents to family or a homeschool group and answers questions. Before moving on, ask: "How should you answer a question you can't answer?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How should you answer a question you can't answer?
questions.a: Say you don't know, explain what you do know, and offer to find out.

days.guide: Child writes a one-page reflection on the research process and improvements. Check understanding with: "Give an example of a specific improvement." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific improvement.
questions.a: 'Start evaluating sources earlier so I don't lose time on unreliable websites.'

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4 levels per trait): Content (thesis and 3 key points with evidence); Visuals (minimal text, image/chart/timeline, all credited); Delivery (eye contact, volume, pacing, few filler words); Time (4.5–5.5 minutes); Q&A (answers accurately or honestly says 'I'd need to check'). Reflection rubric: describes the research process, two strengths, two specific improvements.

weeks.prep: The year's writing portfolio. Prepare the final exam: two unfamiliar passages (one literary, one informational) with 8–10 questions each, a timed argument prompt and 15 grammar/vocabulary items drawn from the year (verbals, voice, mood, punctuation, Greek/Latin roots).
misconceptions: Choosing portfolio pieces by length or neatness rather than growth. Each cover note must name a specific skill the piece shows.
Rushing the timed essay without planning. Spend 5 minutes outlining claim, reasons and evidence.

days.guide: Child selects best narrative, argument, analysis and research pieces and writes a cover note for each explaining the skill it shows. To check, ask: "What should a cover note say?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What should a cover note say?
questions.a: What the assignment was, what skill it shows (e.g., embedding quotations), and what the writer would still improve.

days.guide: Give the reading assessment on unfamiliar passages; no notes. Finish by asking: "A good strategy for a cold read?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A good strategy for a cold read?
questions.a: Preview the questions, read once for the gist, annotate key lines, then return to the text for each answer.

days.guide: Give the timed argument essay (about 45 minutes) and the grammar/vocabulary items. Before moving on, ask: "Label the mood: 'If I were you, I would revise the ending.'" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Label the mood: 'If I were you, I would revise the ending.'
questions.a: Subjunctive ('If I were') with a conditional ('would revise').

days.guide: Child writes a reflection on this year's independent reading and sets summer reading goals. Check understanding with: "What makes a strong reading goal?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What makes a strong reading goal?
questions.a: Specific and measurable — e.g., 'Read four books this summer, including one nonfiction and one classic.'

days.guide: Child reads a favorite piece aloud; discuss growth from September to now using early and late work samples. To check, ask: "Name one way to show growth." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Name one way to show growth.
questions.a: Compare an early paragraph with a later one — e.g., from summarizing quotations to analyzing them.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam: reading — score with your key (main idea, inference, word meaning, structure, author's purpose; answers must cite the passage). Argument essay rubric: claim, evidence, reasoning, counterclaim/rebuttal, organization, conventions (4 levels each). Grammar/vocabulary sample items: identify gerund/participle/infinitive; rewrite passive to active; label indicative/imperative/interrogative/conditional/subjunctive; fix a dangling modifier; punctuate a quotation with an ellipsis; define roots acu- (sharp), cred- (believe), fid- (faith). Portfolio: four pieces (narrative, argument, analysis, research), each with a cover note naming the skill shown.
